title: Jean-luc Doumont Trains Engineers to Present. His First Rule Is That Your Audience Is Never the Problem.
author: Is Public Speaking
summary: This piece distills the core teachings of Jean-luc Doumont, who has trained thousands of engineers and scientists to present, focusing on why technical rooms full of smart people routinely fail to act on presentations they clearly understood. Doumont's key distinction is between information ('what') and a message ('so what') — a slide titled 'Evolution of sales over the years' is a topic, while 'Sales dropped by 40% last year' is a message, and only the latter reliably gets carried out of a room and acted upon. The piece attacks the common chronological presentation structure (motivation, then method, then results, then meaning) as fundamentally audience-blind, since it forces listeners to sit through the presenter's process before reaching the part they actually came for, and cites Doumont's first law directly: if an audience fails to get the message, that is the presenter's problem, not the audience's. The practical exercise offered is writing down, before building any slides, the single sentence you want the audience to remember — check that it is a genuine statement (not a noun phrase like 'Q3 capacity analysis') and lead with it, since professional audiences have almost no tolerance for suspense.
points: The core distinction is information ('what') versus message ('so what') — 'Evolution of sales over the years' is a topic; 'Sales dropped by 40% last year' is a message, and only messages get carried out of a room and acted on.

The common chronological presentation structure (motivation, method, results, meaning) is criticized as audience-blind: it 'focuses on the authors rather than the audience,' forcing listeners to sit through process before reaching the point they came for.

Doumont's first law is stated directly and is described as the one people resist most: if an audience fails to get your message, that is the presenter's problem, not the audience's — a specific academic myth (that a good technical talk should be one-third universally understood, one-third partially understood, one-third opaque) is explicitly rejected as flattering the presenter.
A concrete exercise is offered: before building any slides, write down the single sentence you want the audience to remember, and check that it makes a statement rather than a noun-phrase topic.

Professional audiences are described as having 'almost no tolerance for suspense' — the message should be stated in the first two minutes, modeled on how a mathematician states the theorem before proving it.
quotes: You presented for forty minutes and the room understood every slide... Then a decision got made three weeks later on other grounds, and when you asked why, somebody said they had not realized the finding was that significant. They followed all of it and carried none of it.
Information tells an audience what. A message tells them so what... a message is to information what conclusions are to findings.
Evolution of sales over the years" is a topic. "Sales dropped by 40% last year" is a message, and only one of those two gets carried out of a room.
Adapt to your audience, and he means something harder than it sounds. If they fail to get your message, that is your problem rather than theirs, because you are the one who wanted something.
Prose is architecture, not interior decoration." That is Hemingway, quoted by Doumont, and it is the whole argument about structure compressed into six words.

Ask what one sentence you want remembered. His version: if my audience is to remember only one sentence from my entire presentation, what must it be? Write the answer down before you open a slide deck.
Professional audiences carry almost no tolerance for suspense. They are reading or listening because they need something, and a talk that withholds the conclusion asks them to wait for relevance.
